questions.stem: Which equation represents the Haber process?
options: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ NH₃(g)
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
N₂(g) + H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH(g)
2N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g)
questions.explanation: Nitrogen and hydrogen react in a 1:3 ratio to form two molecules of ammonia, and the reaction is reversible. The forward reaction is exothermic and reduces the number of gas particles from 4 to 2.

questions.stem: Which catalyst is used in the Haber process?
options: Phosphoric acid
Iron
Vanadium(V) oxide
Platinum
questions.explanation: An iron-based catalyst is used to produce ammonia. Vanadium(V) oxide is the catalyst in the contact process, and phosphoric acid catalyses the hydration of ethene.

questions.stem: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) is exothermic. Why is the Haber process run at a moderately high temperature rather than a low one?
options: A high temperature is needed to stop the iron catalyst from melting
A low temperature would shift the equilibrium towards the reactants
A low temperature gives a higher yield, but the rate would be far too slow
A high temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield of ammonia
questions.explanation: Because the forward reaction is exothermic, a lower temperature gives a higher equilibrium yield. But at low temperatures the rate is uneconomically slow, even with a catalyst, so a compromise temperature balances yield against rate.

questions.stem: Why does the Haber process use a high pressure?
options: High pressure is needed to keep the ammonia as a gas so it can be removed
The product side has fewer gas particles, so high pressure raises the yield and the rate
High pressure lowers the activation energy of the forward reaction
The forward reaction is endothermic, so high pressure favours the products
questions.explanation: Four gas particles form two, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right; it also raises the gas concentrations, increasing the rate. Pressure does not change the activation energy, and very high pressures are limited by equipment cost and safety.

questions.stem: An engineer proposes raising the temperature of an ammonia converter from 450 °C to 550 °C, keeping the pressure and catalyst the same. What would be the effect?
options: The rate would decrease, but the equilibrium yield of ammonia and Kc would both increase
The rate would increase, and the equilibrium yield would fall while Kc stays the same
The rate would increase, but the equilibrium yield of ammonia and Kc would both decrease
The rate and the equilibrium yield of ammonia would both increase, and Kc would increase
questions.explanation: A higher temperature increases the rate of both reactions. Because the forward reaction is exothermic, heating shifts the equilibrium to the left, so Kc and the equilibrium yield fall. Temperature is the one change that alters Kc.

questions.stem: In the Haber process, the unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled through the reactor. What is the main benefit?
options: Recycling the gases changes the value of Kc in favour of ammonia
Recycling cools the gases, so the equilibrium shifts to the left
Recycling removes the catalyst poisons from the reaction mixture
Most of the reactants are eventually converted, even though each pass gives a low yield
questions.explanation: Only a fraction of the gases reacts on each pass through the converter. After ammonia is removed by liquefying it, the unreacted gases go back through, so the overall conversion becomes high. Kc depends only on temperature.

questions.stem: Approximate percentage of ammonia at equilibrium: 300 °C and 10 MPa, 52%; 300 °C and 20 MPa, 63%; 400 °C and 10 MPa, 25%; 400 °C and 20 MPa, 36%. Which conclusion do these data support?
options: Yield depends only on temperature, because pressure does not affect gas equilibria
Yield falls with pressure, so fewer gas particles must be on the reactant side
Yield rises with pressure and falls with temperature, so the reaction is exothermic
Yield rises with temperature and falls with pressure, so the reaction is endothermic
questions.explanation: At each temperature the higher pressure gives more ammonia, consistent with fewer gas particles on the product side. At each pressure the higher temperature gives less ammonia, so heating favours the reverse reaction, which means the forward reaction is exothermic.

questions.stem: What is the effect of the catalyst in an industrial process such as the Haber process?
options: It reacts with the nitrogen, so the hydrogen is no longer needed in excess
It lets equilibrium be reached faster at a lower temperature, without changing Kc
It increases the equilibrium yield by shifting the equilibrium to the right
It increases the temperature of the gases, so their particles collide more
questions.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse reactions equally, so the rate rises but the equilibrium position does not change. This allows an economic rate at a lower temperature, where the equilibrium yield is better.

questions.stem: In the contact process, which reaction is carried out over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst?
options: H₂S₂O₇(l) + H₂O(l) → 2H₂SO₄(l)
2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g)
S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)
SO₃(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₄(l)
questions.explanation: The catalytic step is the reversible, exothermic oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide. Burning sulfur to make SO₂ goes to completion without a catalyst, and the later steps convert SO₃ into sulfuric acid.

questions.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) produces fewer gas particles, yet the contact process runs close to atmospheric pressure. Why?
options: The conversion is already very high at low pressure, so extra pressure is not worth the cost
High pressure would shift the equilibrium towards SO₂, lowering the yield
The vanadium(V) oxide catalyst only works below atmospheric pressure
High pressure would make the reaction endothermic and slow it down
questions.explanation: Higher pressure would favour SO₃, but with a catalyst and excess air the conversion is already very high at a little above atmospheric pressure. The small gain in yield would not justify the cost of high-pressure equipment.

questions.stem: In the contact process, SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated sulfuric acid to form oleum, H₂S₂O₇, which is then diluted with water. Why is SO₃ not simply dissolved in water?
options: Water poisons the vanadium(V) oxide catalyst in the same vessel
The reaction with water is so exothermic that a fine mist of acid forms
SO₃ is insoluble in water, so no sulfuric acid would form at all
Water would reduce the SO₃ back to SO₂ and release oxygen gas
questions.explanation: Adding SO₃ directly to water releases so much heat that a corrosive mist of sulfuric acid forms, which is hard to contain. Dissolving it in concentrated sulfuric acid first gives oleum, and H₂S₂O₇ + H₂O → 2H₂SO₄ then produces the acid safely.

questions.stem: 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), ΔH < 0. Which change would increase the equilibrium yield of SO₃?
options: Raising the temperature of the converter
Using a more active catalyst
Increasing the volume of the vessel
Adding more oxygen to the mixture
questions.explanation: Adding a reactant shifts the equilibrium to the right, which is why excess air is used. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, a larger volume favours the side with more gas particles, and a catalyst does not change the yield.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the production of ethanol by fermentation?
options: C₂H₄(g) + H₂O(g) → C₂H₅OH(g)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 3C₂H₅OH(aq)
C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) → 2C₂H₅OH(aq) + 2CO₂(g)
questions.explanation: Yeast enzymes convert glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide in the absence of oxygen. The hydration of ethene is the industrial route from petroleum, and the reaction with oxygen is cellular respiration.

questions.stem: Ethanol is made industrially by the hydration of ethene. Which conditions are used?
options: Steam and a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure
Yeast in a warm sugar solution with no oxygen present
Hydrogen gas and a nickel catalyst at room temperature
Acidified potassium dichromate solution heated under reflux
questions.explanation: Ethene and steam react over a phosphoric acid catalyst at high temperature and pressure: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. Yeast is used in fermentation, hydrogen with nickel reduces alkenes to alkanes, and dichromate would oxidise ethanol.

questions.stem: Why must fermentation of glucose by yeast be kept warm, but not hot, and free of oxygen?
options: High temperatures evaporate the glucose, and oxygen reacts with ethanol to form ethene
Low temperatures denature yeast enzymes, and oxygen is needed to make ethanol
High temperatures denature yeast enzymes, and oxygen lets yeast respire glucose to CO₂ instead
High temperatures shift the equilibrium to the left, and oxygen poisons the catalyst
questions.explanation: Fermentation relies on enzymes, which work fastest at a moderate temperature and are denatured if it is too hot. With oxygen present, yeast carries out aerobic respiration, producing carbon dioxide and water rather than ethanol.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares making ethanol by hydration of ethene with making it by fermentation?
options: Fermentation has the higher atom economy, because it produces no by-product
Hydration is fast and continuous, but uses ethene from non-renewable crude oil
Hydration is slow and done in batches, but uses renewable sugar from crops
Fermentation is fast and continuous, and gives pure ethanol without distillation
questions.explanation: Hydration of ethene is a fast, continuous process giving nearly pure ethanol, but ethene comes from crude oil. Fermentation uses renewable plant sugars, but it is slow, is done in batches, produces CO₂ as a by-product and needs distillation.

questions.stem: What is the atom economy for producing ethanol by fermentation? M: C₆H₁₂O₆ 180.16, C₂H₅OH 46.07 g/mol.
questions.explanation: Atom economy = mass of desired product / total mass of reactants × 100 = (2 × 46.07) / 180.16 × 100 = 51.1%. Using only one ethanol gives 25.6%. Hydration of ethene has an atom economy of 100%, because ethanol is the only product.

questions.stem: 90.0 g of glucose is fermented and 34.5 g of ethanol is obtained. What is the percentage yield? M: C₆H₁₂O₆ 180.16, C₂H₅OH 46.07 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(glucose) = 90.0 / 180.16 = 0.4996 mol, so the theoretical n(ethanol) = 0.999 mol and the theoretical mass is 46.0 g. Yield = 34.5 / 46.0 × 100 = 75.0%. Forgetting the 1:2 ratio gives 150%, and simply dividing 34.5 by 90.0 gives 38.3%.

questions.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, what is the anode half-equation?
options: O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l)
H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻
2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → H₂(g)
H₂(g) → 2H⁺(aq) + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Hydrogen, the fuel, is oxidised at the anode, releasing electrons into the external circuit. In acid it forms H⁺; with an alkaline electrolyte it reacts with OH⁻ to form water instead.

questions.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an alkaline electrolyte, what is the cathode half-equation?
options: 4OH⁻(aq) → O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻
O₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻(aq)
O₂(g) + 4H⁺(aq) + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O(l)
H₂(g) + 2OH⁻(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + 2e⁻
questions.explanation: Oxygen is reduced at the cathode. In alkaline conditions there is very little H⁺, so the half-equation is written with water and hydroxide ions. The version with H⁺ is the cathode reaction in an acidic cell.

questions.stem: Where is water produced in a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, and where in one with an alkaline electrolyte?
options: Acidic: at the cathode. Alkaline: at the anode
Acidic: at the anode. Alkaline: at the cathode
At the cathode in both types of fuel cell
At the anode in both types of fuel cell
questions.explanation: In acid, O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O at the cathode. In alkali, H₂ + 2OH⁻ → 2H₂O + 2e⁻ at the anode (water is also used at the cathode). The overall reaction, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, is the same in both.

questions.stem: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, how does charge move through the electrolyte?
options: H⁺ ions move from the cathode to the anode
H⁺ ions move from the anode to the cathode
Electrons move from the anode to the cathode
OH⁻ ions move from the anode to the cathode
questions.explanation: H⁺ ions formed at the anode travel through the electrolyte to the cathode, where they react with oxygen. Electrons travel through the external circuit, not the electrolyte. In an alkaline cell, OH⁻ ions move from the cathode to the anode.

questions.stem: In a laboratory model of the Haber process, 14.0 g of N₂ reacts with excess H₂ and 3.40 g of NH₃ is collected. What is the percentage yield? M: N₂ 28.02, NH₃ 17.03 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(N₂) = 14.0 / 28.02 = 0.500 mol, so the theoretical n(NH₃) = 1.00 mol, a mass of 17.0 g. Yield = 3.40 / 17.0 × 100 = 20.0%. Forgetting the 1:2 ratio gives 40.0%, and comparing the two masses directly gives 24.3%.

questions.stem: 12.8 g of SO₂ reacts with 4.0 g of O₂: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃. 14.4 g of SO₃ is obtained. What is the percentage yield? M: SO₂ 64.07, O₂ 32.00, SO₃ 80.07 g/mol.
questions.explanation: n(SO₂) = 0.200 mol needs 0.100 mol of O₂, and 0.125 mol is present, so SO₂ is limiting. Theoretical n(SO₃) = 0.200 mol = 16.0 g, and the yield is 14.4 / 16.0 × 100 = 90.0%. Treating O₂ as limiting gives 20.0 g and a yield of 71.9%.

questions.stem: 6.0 g of ethanoic acid (M = 60.05 g/mol) is heated with excess ethanol and an acid catalyst. 5.28 g of ethyl ethanoate (M = 88.11 g/mol) is obtained. What is the percentage yield?
questions.explanation: n(acid) = 6.0 / 60.05 = 0.0999 mol, so the theoretical mass of ester is 0.0999 × 88.11 = 8.80 g. Yield = 5.28 / 8.80 × 100 = 60.0%. Dividing the ester mass by the acid mass gives 88.0%. Esterification is reversible, which is one reason the yield is below 100%.

questions.stem: A two-step synthesis has a yield of 80% for step 1 and 75% for step 2. What is the overall percentage yield?
questions.explanation: The overall yield is the product of the yields: 0.80 × 0.75 = 0.60, or 60%. Averaging the two gives 78%, which overstates the yield because losses accumulate at each step.

questions.stem: To form an addition polymer, a monomer must contain:
options: a carbon-carbon double bond
two different functional groups
an amino group and a carboxyl group
a hydroxyl group at each end
questions.explanation: In addition polymerisation, the C=C double bonds open and the monomers join with no other product. Monomers with two functional groups form condensation polymers instead.

questions.stem: What is the repeating unit of polypropene?
options: -CH₂-CH(CH₃)-
-CH₂-CH₂-CH₂-
-CH=CH-CH₃-
-CH₂-C(CH₃)₂-
questions.explanation: Propene, CH₂=CH-CH₃, adds through its double bond, so the methyl group becomes a side group on every second carbon of the chain. The polymer has no double bonds left, and -CH₂-CH₂-CH₂- is not the structure formed.

questions.stem: Which statement about the formation of polyethene (LDPE or HDPE) and PTFE is correct?
options: Both form by addition polymerisation, with no by-product
Both form by condensation polymerisation, releasing water
Polyethene forms by addition and PTFE by condensation polymerisation
Both need monomers that contain two different functional groups
questions.explanation: Ethene (CH₂=CH₂) and tetrafluoroethene (CF₂=CF₂) both have a C=C double bond that opens to join the monomers, and the polymer is the only product. The conditions used decide whether polyethene forms as LDPE or HDPE.

questions.stem: Condensation polymerisation differs from addition polymerisation because it:
options: releases a small molecule, such as water, each time two monomers join
needs monomers with a carbon-carbon double bond that can open
forms a polymer with the same empirical formula as the monomer
can only produce polymers from a single type of monomer
questions.explanation: Condensation polymers form when functional groups on monomers react and release a small molecule, usually water. Addition polymers form from C=C monomers with no by-product and have the same empirical formula as the monomer.

questions.stem: Nylon-6,6 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid. What kind of link joins the monomers?
options: A carbon-carbon single bond
An amide link, -CO-NH-
An ester link, -CO-O-
A glycosidic link, -C-O-C-
questions.explanation: An amine group reacts with a carboxylic acid group to form an amide link and water, so nylon is a polyamide, like a protein. Ester links join polyesters such as PET and PLA.

questions.stem: Which pair of monomers would react to form a polyester?
options: A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid
An alkene and a haloalkane
A diol and an alkene
A diol and a dicarboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Each -OH group of the diol reacts with a -COOH group of the acid, forming ester links and releasing water. A diamine and a dicarboxylic acid form a polyamide such as nylon.

questions.stem: Polylactic acid (PLA) is made from a single monomer, lactic acid, CH₃CH(OH)COOH. Why can one monomer form a condensation polymer?
options: It has two carboxyl groups, which react with each other to form water
It has an amino group and a carboxyl group, which form amide links
It has both a hydroxyl group and a carboxyl group, which form ester links
It has a C=C double bond, which opens to join the monomers
questions.explanation: The -OH of one lactic acid molecule reacts with the -COOH of the next, forming an ester link and releasing water, so the chain can grow from one monomer. Lactic acid has no double bond and no amino group.

questions.stem: Starch and cellulose are polysaccharides. How do they form?
options: By addition polymerisation of glucose, with no by-product
By condensation of amino acids, joined by peptide links
By condensation of glycerol and fatty acids, joined by ester links
By condensation of glucose monomers, joined by glycosidic links
questions.explanation: Glucose molecules join when an -OH group on one reacts with an -OH group on another, releasing water and forming a C-O-C glycosidic link. Amino acids form proteins, and glycerol and fatty acids form triglycerides.

questions.stem: When three amino acids join to form a tripeptide, how many peptide bonds form and how many water molecules are released?
options: 3 peptide bonds and 2 water molecules
2 peptide bonds and 2 water molecules
3 peptide bonds and 3 water molecules
2 peptide bonds and 3 water molecules
questions.explanation: Each peptide bond forms by condensation between two amino acids and releases one water molecule. Three amino acids in a chain are joined by two bonds, so two water molecules are released.

questions.stem: In the tripeptide written Ala-Gly-Ser, which amino acid has the free amino (-NH₂) group?
options: Serine
Both alanine and serine
Alanine
Glycine
questions.explanation: By convention a peptide is written from the end with the free amino group (the N-terminus) to the end with the free carboxyl group (the C-terminus). So alanine has the free -NH₂ and serine has the free -COOH.

questions.stem: How many different tripeptides can be made from glycine, alanine and serine if each amino acid is used exactly once?
questions.explanation: The first position can be any of 3 amino acids, the second any of the remaining 2, and the third the last one: 3 × 2 × 1 = 6. Gly-Ala-Ser and Ser-Ala-Gly are different tripeptides because the ends differ. 27 would allow repeats.

questions.stem: What is the molar mass of the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Ser? M: glycine 75.07, alanine 89.09, serine 105.09, water 18.02 g/mol.
questions.explanation: Adding the amino acids gives 269.25 g/mol, and forming two peptide bonds removes two water molecules: 269.25 − 2 × 18.02 = 233.21 g/mol. Subtracting only one water gives 251.23 g/mol.

questions.stem: Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁, is a disaccharide. Which monosaccharides form it, and what joins them?
options: Glucose and galactose, joined by a glycosidic bond
Glucose and fructose, joined by a glycosidic bond
Glucose and glucose, joined by a peptide bond
Glucose and fructose, joined by an ester bond
questions.explanation: Glucose and fructose (both C₆H₁₂O₆) condense to form sucrose and water; 2 × 180.16 − 18.02 = 342.30 g/mol, which matches C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Glucose and galactose form lactose, and two glucose units form maltose.

questions.stem: Biodiesel can be made by lipase-catalysed transesterification of plant oils with methanol. What is an advantage of using the enzyme?
options: It is used up in the reaction, so it never needs to be separated
It raises the temperature of the mixture so the reaction is faster
It works at moderate temperatures and gives fewer unwanted by-products
It changes the position of equilibrium so that no glycerol forms
questions.explanation: Enzymes are specific catalysts that work at mild temperatures, reducing energy use and side reactions such as soap formation with base catalysts. Glycerol is still a product of transesterification, and a catalyst does not change the equilibrium.
